title: Classrooms as Dopamine Dispensers: The High Cost of Constant Engagement
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart opens with his wife's summer line to their daughters, that she is not their cruise director, and uses it to confess that schools, himself included, have bent lessons around the lowest level of attention and called it engagement. He describes replacing paper with screens, adding games and songs, and treating boredom as failure, which has produced a model of school that resembles social media. Citing Haidt's account of the phone-based childhood, he argues that schools leaned into the same stimulation they should have resisted. Lenore Skenazy's Let Grow Play Clubs are his example of what happens when adults step back, with calmer, more confident students and fewer referrals. He closes with advice for teachers, parents and school leaders: give students problems worth sitting with, protect boredom and reclaim recess.
points: Constant engagement tools like Kahoot, Gimkit and flashy slide decks train stamina out of students, then adults blame the students for lacking it.
Stinehart's self-implicating confession makes the case that the pursuit of engagement became its own goal without asking what students were engaged in.
Boredom is presented as the precursor to creativity and sustained thought, and so as something schools should protect.
Play Club is offered as the low-cost remedy, reporting less conflict, fewer behavior referrals and calmer students.
The closing advice is concrete: harder problems, more recess, and fewer engagement hacks.
quotes: We thought more excitement meant more learning, more busyness meant more growth, and the more high-octane the lesson was the more substance it had. And I’ll be the first to admit: I’ve done the same thing in my classroom.
I’ve designed lessons around short attention spans. I’ve replaced boring paper with flashy screens, structure with slide decks, stamina with speed.
Because somewhere along the line, we started treating boredom like failure. And so we built a system to avoid it at all costs.

Because if we only ever teach them to expect engagement and entertainment, we’ve failed to teach them how to push through boredom and frustration. We’ve failed to teach them the beauty of sustained thought, the dignity of delayed gratification, and the reward of hard work that doesn’t come with a prize, a badge, or an award.

And the more we did it, the more we created a model of school that looks and feels like social media - short bursts, fast-paced, flashy wins, and surface-level thinking. And then we wonder why kids can’t stay with a singular thought.
We don’t need another program. We don’t need more tech. We don’t need to invent another system of rewards. We need to trust kids enough to let go and let them be kids.
This isn’t a call to lower expectations. It’s a call to raise them in the right direction. We don’t need more engagement hacks.
